'''Seymour Benzer''' (October 15, 1921 – November 30, 2007) was an American [[physicist]], [[molecular biologist]] and [[behavioral geneticist]]. His career began during the molecular biology revolution of the 1950s, and he eventually rose to prominence in the fields of molecular and behavioral genetics. He led a productive genetics research lab both at Purdue University and as the James G. Boswell Professor of Neuroscience, emeritus, at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name="frs">{{Cite journal | last1 = Greenspan | first1 = R. J. | doi = 10.1098/rsbm.2012.0031 | title = Seymour Benzer. 15 October 1921 -- 30 November 2007 | journal = [[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] | year = 2012 | volume=58 | pages=23–32| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name="Greenspan 2008 R106–10">{{Cite journal | last1 = Greenspan | first1 = R. J. | title = Seymour Benzer (1921–2007) | doi = 10.1016/j.cub.2007.12.039 | journal = Current Biology | volume = 18 | issue = 3 | pages = R106–R110 | year = 2008 | pmid =  18345547| s2cid = 2094146 | doi-access = free | bibcode = 2008CBio...18.R106G }}</ref><ref name=nytzimmer>{{cite news | author=Carl Zimmer | title=Seymour Benzer, geneticist, is dead at 86 | work=The New York Times| url=https://www.nytimes.com/2007/12/08/science/08benzer.html?ref=science | date=8 December 2007 | access-date=2008-02-18| author-link=Carl Zimmer }}</ref>

==Biography==

===Early life and education===
Benzer was born in the [[South Bronx]] to Meir Benzer and Eva Naidorf, both Jews from Poland.<ref>{{cite web |title=Interview with Seymour Benzer |url=https://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechOH:OH_Benzer_S |website=CaltechOralHistories |date=January 2002 |access-date=28 June 2024}}</ref> He had two older sisters, and his parents favored him as the only boy.<ref name="Holmes"/> One of Benzer's earliest scientific experiences was dissecting frogs he had caught as a boy. In an interview at Caltech, Benzer also remembered receiving a microscope for his 13th birthday, "and that opened up the whole world."<ref name="oralhistory">{{cite web|last=Benzer|first=Seymour|title=Seymour Benzer (1921-2007) Interviewed by Heidi Asputrian|url=http://resolver.caltech.edu/CaltechOH:OH_Benzer_S|work=Oral History Project|publisher=California Institute of Technology Archives|access-date=19 April 2011|year=1991}}</ref> The book ''[[Arrowsmith (novel)|Arrowsmith]]'' by [[Sinclair Lewis]] heavily influenced the young Benzer, and he even imitated the handwriting of Max Gottlieb, a scientist character in the novel. Benzer graduated from [[New Utrecht High School]] at 15 years old.<ref name="Weiner"/>

In 1938 he enrolled at [[Brooklyn College]] where he majored in physics.<ref name=nytzimmer/> Benzer then moved on to [[Purdue University]] to earn his Ph.D. in solid state physics. While there he was recruited for a secret military project to develop improved radar. He performed research that led to the development of stable [[germanium]] rectifiers and discovered a germanium crystal able to be used at high voltages, among the scientific work that led to the first [[transistor]].<ref name="Greenspan 2008 R106–10"/><ref name="nytzimmer"/><ref name="caltechobit">{{cite press release |title=Neurogenetics Pioneer Seymour Benzer Dies |url=http://mr.caltech.edu/media/Press_Releases/PR13076.html |publisher=California Institute of Technology |date=30 November 2007 |access-date=2008-02-18 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080208080709/http://mr.caltech.edu/media/Press_Releases/PR13076.html |archive-date=8 February 2008 }}</ref>

===Personal life===
At [[Brooklyn College]], as a sixteen-year-old freshman, Benzer met Dorothy Vlosky (nicknamed Dotty), a twenty-one-year-old [[nurse]]. He later married her in [[New York City]] in 1942.<ref name="Weiner" /> They had two daughters.

Benzer died of a stroke at the [[Huntington Hospital]] in [[Pasadena, California]].<ref name=caltechobit />

==Scientific career==

===Molecular biology===

Upon receiving his Ph.D. in 1947, he was immediately hired as an assistant professor in physics at Purdue. However, Benzer was inspired by [[Erwin Schrödinger]]'s book ''[[What Is Life?]]'', in which the physicist pondered the physical nature of the gene and a "code" of life. This catalyzed Benzer's shift in interest to biology, and he moved into the area of [[bacteriophage]] genetics.,<ref name="Retros">{{Cite journal | last1 = Jan | first1 = Y. -N. | last2 = Jan | first2 = L. | doi = 10.1126/science.1154050 | title = Retrospective: Seymour Benzer (1921-2007) | journal = Science | volume = 319 | issue = 5859 | pages = 45 | year = 2008 | pmid = 18174427| s2cid = 206511019 }}</ref> spending two years as a postdoctoral fellow in [[Max Delbrück]]'s laboratory at California Institute of Technology, and then returning to Purdue. At Purdue University, Benzer developed the [[T4 rII system|T4 ''rII'' system]], a new genetic technique involving [[Genetic recombination|recombination]] in T4 bacteriophage ''rII'' mutants.<ref name="topography">{{Cite journal | last1 = Benzer | first1 = S. | author-link1 = Seymour Benzer| title = On the Topography of the Genetic Fine Structure | doi = 10.1073/pnas.47.3.403 | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 47 | issue = 3 | pages = 403–415 | year = 1961 | pmid =  16590840| pmc = 221592|bibcode = 1961PNAS...47..403B | doi-access = free }}</ref> After observing that a particular ''rII'' mutant, a mutation that caused the bacteriophage to eliminate bacteria more rapidly than usual, was not exhibiting the expected phenotype, it occurred to Benzer that this strain might have come from a cross between two different ''rII'' mutants (each having part of the ''rII'' gene intact) wherein a [[genetic recombination|recombination]] event resulted in a normal ''rII'' sequence.  Benzer realized that by generating many ''r'' mutants and recording the [[recombination frequency]] between different ''r'' strains, one could create a detailed map of the gene, much as [[Alfred Sturtevant]] had done for [[chromosomes]].<ref name=Weiner /> Taking advantage of the enormous number of recombinants that could be analyzed in the ''rII'' mutant system, Benzer was eventually able to map over 2400 ''rII'' mutations. The data he collected provided the first evidence that the gene is not an indivisible entity, as previously believed, and that genes were linear.<ref name="topology">{{Cite journal | last1 = Benzer | first1 = S. | author-link = Seymour Benzer| title = On the Topology of the Genetic Fine Structure | doi = 10.1073/pnas.45.11.1607 | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 45 | issue = 11 | pages = 1607–20 | year = 1959 | pmid =  16590553| pmc = 222769|bibcode = 1959PNAS...45.1607B | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref name=topography />   Benzer also proved that [[mutation]]s were distributed in many different parts of a single gene, and the resolving power of his system allowed him to discern mutants that differ at the level of a single [[nucleotide]].  Based on his ''rII'' data, Benzer also proposed distinct classes of mutations including [[deletion (genetics)|deletions]], [[point mutations]], [[missense mutations]], and [[nonsense mutations]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Jayaraman, R. Reson|title=Seymour Benzer and T4 ''r''II: Running the Map into the Ground|journal=Resonance|year=2008|pages=898–908|doi=10.1007/s12045-008-0098-6|url=http://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/reso/013/10/0898-0908|volume=13|issue=10|s2cid=84968274|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Benzer's work influenced many other scientists of his time (see [[Phage group]]). In his molecular biology period, Benzer dissected the fine structure of a single gene, laying down the ground work for decades of mutation analysis and genetic engineering, and setting up a paradigm using the ''rII'' phage that would later be used by [[Francis Crick]] and [[Sydney Brenner]] to establish the [[triplet code]] of [[DNA]]. In addition, Benzer's mapping technique was taken up by [[Richard Feynman]].<ref name="Weiner" />

In 1967, Benzer left the field of phage genetics and returned to the California Institute of Technology to work in [[behavioral genetics]].

===Behavioral genetics===

====Benzer vs. Hirsch====
Benzer was one of the first scientists to rise to prominence in the field of [[behavioral genetics]]. As the field began to emerge in the 1960s and 70s, Benzer found himself in scientific opposition to another of the field's leading researchers, [[Jerry Hirsch]]. While Hirsch believed that behaviors were complex phenomena irreducible to the level of single genes, Benzer advocated that animal behaviors were not too complex to be directed by a single gene. This translated to methodological differences in the two researchers' experiments with [[Drosophila]] (fruit flies) that profoundly influenced the field of behavioral genetics. Hirsch artificially selected for behaviors of interest over many generations, while Benzer primarily used [[forward genetics|forward genetic]] mutagenesis screens to isolate mutants for a particular behavior.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Tully | first1 = T. | title = Discovery of genes involved with learning and memory: An experimental synthesis of Hirschian and Benzerian perspectives | doi = 10.1073/pnas.93.24.13460 | journal = Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume = 93 | issue = 24 | pages = 13460–13467 | year = 1996 | pmid =  8942957| pmc = 33631|bibcode = 1996PNAS...9313460T | doi-access = free }}</ref> Benzer and Hirsch's competing philosophies served to provide necessary scientific tension in order to accelerate and enhance developments in behavioral genetics, helping it gain traction as a legitimate area of study in the scientific community.

====Research accomplishments====
Benzer used forward genetics to investigate the genetic basis of various behaviors such as [[phototaxis]], [[circadian rhythms]], and learning by inducing mutations in a Drosophila population and then screening individuals for altered phenotypes of interest.<ref name="Retros"/> To better identify mutants, Benzer developed novel apparatuses such as the countercurrent device, which was designed to separate flies according to the magnitude and direction of their phototactic response.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Bonini | first1=N. M. | title=A Tribute to Seymour Benzer, 1921-2007 | doi=10.1534/genetics.104.97782 | journal=Genetics | volume=180 | issue=3 | pages=1265–1273 | year=2008 | pmid= 19001297| pmc =2581933 }}</ref> Benzer identified mutants for a wide variety of characteristics: vision (''nonphototactic'', ''negative phototactic'', and ''eyes absent''<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Bonini | first1=N. M. | last2=Leiserson | first2=W. M. | last3=Benzer | first3=S. | author-link3=Seymour Benzer| doi=10.1016/0092-8674(93)90115-7 | title=The eyes absent gene: Genetic control of cell survival and differentiation in the developing Drosophila eye | journal=Cell | volume=72 | issue=3 | pages=379–395 | year=1993 | pmid= 8431945| s2cid=36882227 }}</ref>), locomotion (''sluggish'', ''uncoordinated''), stress sensitivity (''freaked-out''), sexual function (''savoir-faire'', ''[[fruitless (gene)|fruitless]]''), nerve and muscle function (''photoreceptor degeneration'', ''drop-dead''), learning, and memory (''[[Rutabaga (gene)|rutabaga]]'', ''dunce''<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Dudai | first1=Y. | last2=Jan | first2=Y. N. | last3=Byers | first3=D. | last4=Quinn | first4=W. G. | last5=Benzer | first5=S. | title=Dunce, a Mutant of Drosophila Deficient in Learning | doi=10.1073/pnas.73.5.1684 | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=73 | issue=5 | pages=1684–1688 | year=1976 | pmid= 818641| pmc=430364|bibcode=1976PNAS...73.1684D | url=http://authors.library.caltech.edu/9215/1/DUDpnas76.pdf | doi-access=free }}</ref>).<ref name="genetobehavior">{{Cite journal | last1=Benzer | first1=S. | author-link1=Seymour Benzer| title=From the Gene to Behavior | doi=10.1001/jama.1971.03190200047010 | journal=JAMA: The Journal of the American Medical Association | volume=218 | issue=7 | pages=1015–1022 | year=1971 | pmid=4942064 }}</ref>

Benzer and student [[Ron Konopka]] discovered the first circadian rhythm mutants. Three distinct mutant types—arrhythmic, shortened period, and lengthened period—were identified. These mutations all involved the same functional gene on the X chromosome and influenced the eclosion rhythm of the population as well as rhythms in individual flies' locomotor activity.<ref name="perMutants">{{Cite journal | last1=Konopka | first1=R. J. | last2=Benzer | first2=S. | title=Clock Mutants of Drosophila melanogaster | doi=10.1073/pnas.68.9.2112 | journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences | volume=68 | issue=9 | pages=2112–2116 | year=1971 | pmid= 5002428| pmc=389363|bibcode=1971PNAS...68.2112K | doi-access=free }}</ref> To monitor ''Drosophila'' locomotor activity, Benzer and postdoctoral researcher, Yoshiki Hotta, designed a system using [[infrared light]] and [[Solar cell|solar cells]].<ref name="perMutants" /> All three mutations were mapped to the X chromosome, zero centimorgans away from each other, indicating that the mutant phenotypes corresponded to alleles of the same gene, which Konopka named ''[[period (gene)|period]]''.<ref name="perMutants" /> This was the first of several seminal studies of single genes affecting behavior, studies that have been replicated in other animal models and are now the basis for the growing field of molecular biology of behavior. In 1992 Benzer, working with Michael Rosbash, furthered this work by showing that the PER protein, which ''[[period (gene)|period]]'' codes for, is predominantly located in the nucleus.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Liu | first1=X. | last2=Zwiebel | first2=L. J. | last3=Hinton | first3=D.
| last4=Benzer | first4=S. | author-link4=Seymour Benzer| last5=Hall | first5=J. C. | last6=Rosbash | first6=M. | title=The period gene encodes a predominantly nuclear protein in adult Drosophila | journal=The Journal of Neuroscience | volume=12 | issue=7 | pages=2735–2744 | year=1992 | pmid=1613555| pmc=6575836 | doi=10.1523/JNEUROSCI.12-07-02735.1992 }}</ref> The work with Period mutants was catalytic in the study of circadian rhythms and served to propel the field forward.

On 2 October 2017, Dr. Rosbash, along with Drs. Michael W. Young and Jeffrey C. Hall, were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in recognition of their cloning of circadian rhythm genes, and the elucidation of the [[biochemical]] mechanisms by which the circadian rhythm protein products [[regulated behavior]].

Benzer was at the forefront of the study of neurodegeneration in fruit flies, modeling human [[Disease|diseases]] and attempting to suppress them. He also contributed to the field of aging biology, looking for mutants with altered longevity and trying to dissect the mechanisms by which an [[organism]] can escape the inevitable functional downfall and its associated diseases.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://ouroboros.wordpress.com/2007/12/03/would-that-he-were-methuselah-seymour-benzer-1921-2007/ | title=Would that he were Methuselah: Seymour Benzer, 1921-2007 | work=Ouroboros | date=2007-12-03 | access-date=2007-12-07}}</ref> In 1998, Benzer and his colleagues Yi-Jyun Lin and Laurent Seroude published findings of a long-life mutant in ''Drosophila'', then named Methuselah. The mutant gene coded for a previously unknown member of the [[GPCR]] family. By testing against temperature stress, it is thought that these mutants have an increased ability to respond to stress and thus to live longer.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Lin | first1=Y. | last2=Seroude | first2=L. | last3=Benzer | first3=S. | author-link3=Seymour Benzer| doi=10.1126/science.282.5390.943 | title=Extended Life-Span and Stress Resistance in the Drosophila Mutant methuselah | journal=Science | volume=282 | issue=5390 | pages=943–946 | year=1998 | pmid= 9794765|bibcode=1998Sci...282..943L | s2cid=43149680 }}</ref> One of Benzer's final research projects was on [[dietary restriction]] and [[longevity]] research. A paper was published, in '[[Cell magazine|'Cell']]', on the longevity effect of 4E-BP, a translational repressor, following dietary restriction. Although the research was done before his [[death]], the paper was published afterwards and dedicated to his memory.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Zid | first1=B. M. | last2=Rogers | first2=A. N. | last3=Katewa | first3=S. D. | last4=Vargas | first4=M. A. | last5=Kolipinski | first5=M. C. | last6=Lu | first6=T. A. | last7=Benzer | first7=S. | author-link7=Seymour Benzer| last8=Kapahi | first8=P. | doi=10.1016/j.cell.2009.07.034 | title=4E-BP Extends Lifespan upon Dietary Restriction by Enhancing Mitochondrial Activity in Drosophila | journal=Cell | volume=139 | issue=1 | pages=149–160 | year=2009 | pmid= 19804760| pmc =2759400 }}</ref>


===Cancer research===

In 1978, Dotty was in the hospital with breast cancer, and Seymour's friend, colleague, and mentor [[Max Delbrück]] was diagnosed with cancer. Consequently, Seymour Benzer took interest in cancer biology and attended several conferences on breast cancer.<ref name="Weiner" />
Benzer later remarried with Carol Miller, a [[neuropathology|neuropathologist]]. Together, in the early 1980s, they used [[immunostaining|antibody staining]] techniques to find nearly identical [[genes]] between flies and humans.<ref name="Weiner" />

==Books==
Benzer is the subject of the 1999 book ''[[Time, Love, Memory]]: A Great Biologist and His Quest for the Origins of Behavior'' by [[Pulitzer Prize|Pulitzer laureate]] [[Jonathan Weiner]],<ref name="Weiner">{{cite book | last=Weiner | first=Jonathan | title=Time, Love, Memory: A Great Biologist and His Quest for the Origins of Behavior | location=New York | publisher=Knopf | year=1999 | isbn=978-0-679-44435-0 | url-access=registration | url=https://archive.org/details/timelovememorygr00wein }}</ref> and ''Reconceiving the Gene: Seymour Benzer's Adventures in Phage Genetics'' by Lawrence Holmes.<ref name="Holmes">{{cite book | last=Holmes | first=Frederic Lawrence |author2=Summers, William C. | title=Reconceiving the Gene: Seymour Benzer's Adventures in Phage Genetics | location=New Haven | publisher=Yale University Press | year=2006 | isbn=978-0-300-11078-4 }}</ref>
